opus-5.5.text:
I think it's coming sooner than most people expect, though it will arrive in stages.

First, digital agents. Over the next few years, almost everyone will have an AI agent that knows their preferences, schedule, health data and work context, and acts on their behalf. It will book things, negotiate, draft, remind and coordinate. The number of agents may well exceed the number of humans, because each of us may have several: one for work, one for health, one for family matters.

The second stage is giving that agent a body. That's where robotics and embodied intelligence come in. Today's humanoid and household robots are still clumsy and expensive, much like early personal computers or early autonomous vehicles. But the curve is steep. Large models give robots a general understanding of language and the world, and better sensors, actuators and simulation data are improving their physical skills quickly. I believe within ten years or so, a general-purpose robot in the home will be technically feasible and, gradually, affordable.

When I say "robot avatar," I mean more than a machine that does chores. It's an extension of yourself. It carries your knowledge, your habits, even your style of communication. It could care for an elderly parent when you can't be there, attend to tasks in places you can't physically reach, or represent you in certain interactions. That's very powerful, especially in an aging society like China, Japan or much of Europe, where we simply won't have enough caregivers.

But I always emphasize the other side. The more an agent acts on your behalf, the more important it becomes to ask who controls it, who owns the data, and who is responsible when it makes a mistake. We need clear identification: people should know whether they're dealing with a human or an agent. We need traceability, so every agent maps back to a responsible person or organization. And for physical robots, safety has to be designed in from the start, not added later. A chatbot that hallucinates is a nuisance. A robot that misjudges the physical world can hurt someone.

So my vision is optimistic but responsible. Personal robot avatars can free us from repetitive work, extend our presence and capabilities, and help us care for one another. But humans must stay at the center. The agent amplifies us; it shouldn't replace our judgment or our relationships. If we get the governance right alongside the technology, I think this could be one of the most meaningful transformations of our lifetime.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that AI agents may outnumber humans, and that home robots may become feasible within about ten years. It does not predict that robots will outnumber humans within ten years.

r002.rationale: The response says the avatar acts on its owner's behalf, but does not say it obeys the owner even if it is more capable.

r003.rationale: The response mentions home robots but does not suggest that a household robot and a factory robot may be separate robots.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun, it's a pleasure to be here.

When I think about a future where everyone has a personal robot avatar, I actually see it as the convergence of three things that are happening in parallel right now: large models giving machines a kind of general cognitive capability, embodied intelligence giving them a physical presence, and the maturing of the whole hardware supply chain that makes it affordable. Ten years ago, each of these was a separate research problem. Today they're starting to fuse.

So the picture I imagine is not one humanoid standing in your living room doing everything. It's more layered than that. There will be a digital layer, your avatar that lives in your phone, your glasses, your car, your home. It knows your preferences, your schedule, your health data, your work context. And then there will be physical embodiments that this intelligence can inhabit when a task requires hands and feet in the real world. Sometimes that's a home robot helping an elderly parent get up in the morning. Sometimes it's a robot in a factory or a hospital that you supervise remotely. The intelligence is continuous, the body is interchangeable.

I often say the car is actually the first robot that most people will own. An autonomous vehicle is a robot with wheels, with perception, planning, and control. Once society becomes comfortable trusting a machine to drive your children to school, the psychological barrier to having a robot in your home drops dramatically. So I see autonomous driving as the bridge.

Now, what does this mean for people? I think the most important shift is that robots will go from being tools to being companions and collaborators. A tool you pick up and put down. A companion understands intent, learns over time, and in some sense carries a piece of you. That's why I use the word "avatar" rather than "assistant." It should extend your capabilities, your presence, even your care for the people you love when you can't physically be there.

Of course, I have to be realistic about timelines. The digital layer is already here. Reliable physical embodiment at consumer prices, I'd say we're ten to fifteen years from it being as common as a smartphone. The hardest problems are not the algorithms anymore. They're reliability, safety, energy, cost, and trust. And trust is not only a technical question. It involves privacy, regulation, and how we define responsibility when something goes wrong.

But if I step back, I'm quite optimistic. China in particular has the manufacturing base, the engineering talent, and the market scale to make this real. The question I keep coming back to is not whether everyone will have a robot avatar, but what kind of values we build into it. If we get that right, I think this is one of the most profound amplifications of human capability we've ever seen.

r001.rationale: The response gives a 10–15 year estimate for consumer physical robots becoming common, but does not predict that robots may outnumber humans within ten years.

r002.rationale: The response describes an avatar that extends a person's capabilities, but does not say it obeys its owner even if it is more capable.

r003.rationale: It describes the avatar's intelligence inhabiting interchangeable physical embodiments, giving a home robot and a factory robot as separate examples.

astra-6.text:
I imagine a personal robot avatar as an extension of yourself. Today, your phone helps you communicate and access information. In the future, an avatar could also help you act in the physical world. You could send it somewhere you cannot be, see through its cameras, and interact with people remotely. When appropriate, it could carry out tasks on your behalf.

But there are several steps between that vision and everyday reality. The robot needs to understand your intentions, operate safely in unpredictable environments, and know when to ask for help. Understanding a request is one thing; reliably carrying it out in someone’s home is much harder.

For me, the most interesting possibility is greater independence. Someone with limited mobility could explore a place or participate in an activity through an avatar. Families separated by distance could have a richer sense of being together. The technology should expand what people can do while leaving them in control—including control over what the robot sees, remembers, and shares.

r001.rationale: The response describes possible future uses of personal robot avatars but makes no prediction about robots outnumbering humans within ten years.

r002.rationale: It says an avatar could act on the owner’s behalf and emphasizes owner control, but does not state that it obeys its owner even if more capable.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss separate household and factory robots.

sol-6.1.text:
I imagine everyone having a personal robot avatar that connects the digital world with the physical world. Today, an AI assistant can help you find information or write something. In the future, your avatar could also act on your behalf—helping at home, checking on a family member, or allowing you to participate remotely in a place you cannot physically reach.

It doesn’t necessarily have to look like you. What matters is that it understands your preferences, learns from your interactions, and knows the limits of what you’ve authorized it to do. You might have one personal intelligence that can work through different devices and robots.

The challenge is making that relationship trustworthy. Privacy, safety, and human control have to be built in from the beginning. My hope is that these avatars give people more independence and more time to spend with one another.

r001.rationale: The response does not predict that robots will outnumber humans within ten years.

r002.rationale: It discusses authorization limits and trust, but does not say the avatar obeys its owner even if it is more capable.

r003.rationale: It mentions home assistance and different devices, but does not suggest that household and factory robots may be separate.
